## Original idea
{
  "title": "Oracle-Free Expert Iteration for Autoformalization via BEq+ Consensus and Generator-Verifier Co-Evolution",
  "core_problem": "Current autoformalization training pipelines rely on LLM semantic judges at critical quality-gating steps, introducing false-positive rates that are poorly characterized and potentially compound across iterative training. ReForm (ICLR 2026), the current training-time SOTA, uses CriticLean-14B rewards during RL and Qwen3-235B-generated SFT trajectories, achieving 70.4% LLM-judged semantic consistency on ProofNet—but its ConsistencyCheck benchmark reveals that even the best LLM judges achieve only 79–86% accuracy on binary semantic classification, and different judges yield substantially different evaluations of identical outputs (CriticLean-14B: 70.3% average vs. Qwen3-235B: 72.7% for the same ReForm-32B model). ATLAS (NeurIPS 2025) runs 10 rounds of expert iteration with DeepSeek-V3 alignment ratings but admits 17.2% major errors among judge-approved formalizations. StepFun-Formalizer (AAAI 2026) uses BEq equivalence class partitioning with exact? only (BEqL) but applies this one-shot, not iteratively. Can we build a fully oracle-free, iteratively self-improving autoformalization loop where BEq+ consensus among the model's own candidates—with provably zero false positives and augmented by generator-verifier co-evolution to combat consensus collapse—serves as both quality filter and training signal, producing formally higher-fidelity training data that yields superior downstream theorem-proving performance despite potentially lower data volume than LLM-judge-filtered approaches?",
  "opportunity": "ReForm (ICLR 2026) demonstrates that integrating semantic self-reflection into autoformalization training yields dramatic improvements (22.6pp average over baselines), but its approach has three structural limitations that our work exploits. First, judge unreliability: ReForm's own ConsistencyCheck benchmark shows the best LLM judge (Gemini-2.5-Pro) achieves only 85.8% accuracy on binary semantic classification, with precision ranging from 75.5% to 88.9%—and ReForm's RL training uses CriticLean-14B, which scores only 79.1% on this same benchmark. For training data quality-gating, these error rates mean 14–21% of reward signals are incorrect. Second, judge inconsistency: different judges yield substantially different scores for identical outputs (CriticLean-14B vs. Qwen3-235B differ by ~2.4pp average on ReForm-32B), creating systematic evaluation uncertainty with no formal ground truth. Third, single-round training: ReForm performs one round of SFT + RL (on 447K trajectories and 2K RL problems), not iterative expert iteration—leaving the potential for self-improving loops unexplored. BEq+ consensus addresses all three limitations. BEq+ (Poiroux et al., EMNLP 2025) extends BEqL (exact? only, as used by StepFun-Formalizer) with additional decision tactics (simp, ring, omega, linarith, norm_num), substantially improving recall over BEqL while maintaining the fundamental soundness guarantee: if a formal tactic proves two Lean 4 statements equivalent, they ARE equivalent—100% precision by construction, not by empirical estimate. Liu et al. (ICLR 2025 Spotlight) demonstrated that BEq achieves 100% precision and 90.50% accuracy on 200 expert-annotated pairs, compared to 70.59% precision and 82.50% accuracy for prior non-formal metrics. BEq+'s expanded tactic set further improves recall (the ability to detect true equivalences that BEqL's exact? alone misses), addressing the concern raised by Li et al. (NeurIPS 2024) that ATPs are 'far from capable' and by StepFun's BEq@1-to-BEq@16 gap (40.5% vs. 59.3%) revealing many correct candidates that strict BEqL cannot verify. The core testable hypothesis: BEq+-filtered training signal has provably zero false positives, and when used iteratively with generator-verifier co-evolution, this formal fidelity advantage over LLM-judge-filtered training yields: (a) lower false-positive formalization rates at each round, (b) no accumulation of semantic errors across iterations (unlike LLM-judge pipelines), and (c) superior downstream theorem-proving success per training example. Even if BEq+ produces smaller training sets than LLM judges, GRPO-based RL can learn effectively from limited high-fidelity data (FormaRL: 859 samples yielded 4–6× improvement).",
  "landscape": "Training-time SOTA — ReForm (ICLR 2026, Chen et al.): Reflective autoformalization with Prospective Bounded Sequence Optimization (PBSO). Based on Qwen3 (8B/32B), trained with single-round SFT on 447K trajectories (generated via Qwen3-235B multi-agent system) followed by RL with PBSO on 2,048 problems using CriticLean-14B rewards. PBSO applies position-specific rewards (task reward at sequence end, auxiliary faithfulness rewards at intermediate critique steps). Achieves: ReForm-8B: 87.7% miniF2F / 65.6% ProofNet / 57.3% PutnamBench; ReForm-32B: 91.4% / 70.4% / 62.3% / 66.7% AIME2025 (all Qwen3-235B-judged). Human evaluation verified 86.1% of miniF2F and 69.4% of ProofNet formalizations as correct. Critical limitation: no compilation-only ablation, so the contribution of formal verification vs. LLM judgment remains unclear. ConsistencyCheck benchmark (859 expert-annotated items) reveals LLM judge accuracy of only 79.1% (CriticLean-14B) to 85.8% (Gemini-2.5-Pro), with precision 75.5%–88.9%. Iterative expert iteration — ATLAS (NeurIPS 2025): 10 rounds of expert iteration using Lean compilation + DeepSeek-V3 semantic alignment rating, generating 117K parallel statements, fine-tuning Llama3.1-8B with LoRA. Achieves 39.46% pass@1 on ProofNet, 23.16% on PutnamBench. Human evaluation reveals 17.2% major errors and 17.2% minor errors among 151 judge-approved formalizations—a non-trivial false-positive rate that compounds over 10 iterative rounds. No ablation removing the LLM judge. One-shot BEq curation — StepFun-Formalizer (AAAI 2026): BEq equivalence class partitioning among 16 candidates using strict BEqL (exact? only) during one-shot data curation from Kimina-Autoformalizer outputs (256K→183K pairs), then BEq-rewarded GRPO on 5.8K examples. Achieves 40.5% BEq@1 on FormalMATH-Lite (BEq@16=59.3%). The 18.8pp gap between BEq@1 and BEq@16 reveals that many correct formalizations exist among the 16 candidates but strict BEqL cannot verify them, motivating expanded tactic sets. Inference-time refinement — Monotonic Reference-Free Refinement (Zhang, Valentino & Freitas, arXiv Jan 2026): Reference-free iterative monotonic process at inference time using theorem prover feedback + LLM-based judges for Formal Validity, Logical Preservation, Mathematical Consistency, and Formal Quality. Achieves 100% formal validity / 90.27% overall on miniF2F, 77.96% / 52.45% on ProofNet. Guarantees certified monotonic improvement per iteration via acceptance policy. Key distinction: inference-time only (not training-time), and still uses LLM judges for semantic dimensions—thus oracle-dependent in the semantic fidelity sense. BEq metrics hierarchy: Liu et al. (ICLR 2025 Spotlight) introduced BEq using tactics {apply, cases', constructor, exact, exact?, ext, have, intro, intros, rw, use}, achieving 100% precision and 90.50% accuracy vs. 70.59%/82.50% for prior non-formal metrics on 200 annotated pairs. BEqL is the strict variant using only exact? (as used by StepFun-Formalizer). Poiroux et al. (EMNLP 2025) introduced BEq+, adding simp, ring, omega, linarith, norm_num to improve recall on 3,752 ProofNetVerif annotations, correlating strongly with human judgment. Full hierarchy: BEqL (lowest recall, highest speed) → BEq (medium) → BEq+ (highest recall, same 100% precision by Lean kernel soundness). RL for autoformalization — FormaRL (COLM 2025): GRPO with compilation + LLM semantic consistency boosted ProofNet from 4% to 26% with only 859 unlabeled samples—demonstrating RL's superiority over SFT with limited formal data. Consensus collapse — CoVerRL (ACL 2026): Identifies the 'consensus trap' in label-free reasoning and proposes generator-verifier co-evolution with balanced contrastive data; achieves 4.7–5.9% gains, improves self-verification accuracy from ~55% to >85%. RL Tango (NeurIPS 2025) independently proposes concurrent generator-verifier RL training, achieving 25.5% relative improvement. Formalization faithfulness — 'Do LLMs Game Formalization?' (VerifAI-2 Workshop, ICLR 2026): Evaluates GPT-5 and DeepSeek-R1 on 303 FOL problems. Finds 59 axiom fabrications by GPT-5, but critically these occur only in the two-stage pipeline (where formalization and proving are separated)—in unified generation (closer to autoformalization), the paper finds 'no evidence of systematic gaming.' More relevant to our setting: the paper concludes that 'high compilation rates should not be equated with faithful reasoning,' reinforcing the need for semantic verification beyond compilation. Self-verification theory: Gerstgrasser et al. (NeurIPS 2025) prove self-verification prevents model collapse but show verifier-based retraining converges to the verifier's 'knowledge center'—motivating our co-evolution strategy. Li et al. (NeurIPS 2024) use symbolic equivalence among k candidates with 12 tactics for inference-time reranking. TinyV (2025) reports >38% false negatives in rule-based verification, motivating expanded tactic sets. NSRSA (arXiv 2026) stabilizes iterative self-training via symbolic verification gating. The unexplored combination: No prior work applies BEq+ consensus iteratively in a training loop with generator-verifier co-evolution. ReForm is single-round. ATLAS iterates but with LLM judges. StepFun uses BEq but one-shot with BEqL only. Our contribution fills this gap.",
  "inspired_by": "ReForm's single-round SFT+RL achieving current SOTA (but with 79–86% judge accuracy on ConsistencyCheck) + ATLAS's expert iteration (10 rounds, but 17.2% major error rate in LLM-judged outputs) + StepFun-Formalizer's BEq equivalence class partitioning (BEq@16=59.3%, but one-shot with BEqL only) + CoVerRL's generator-verifier co-evolution for breaking consensus traps + RL Tango's concurrent generator-verifier training + FormaRL's GRPO with 859 samples outperforming SFT + Liu et al.'s BEq with 100% precision (ICLR 2025 Spotlight) + Poiroux et al.'s BEq+ extending recall via expanded tactics (EMNLP 2025) + Li et al.'s finding that ATPs are 'far from capable' (motivating BEq+ over strict BEqL) + Gerstgrasser et al.'s convergence-to-verifier-knowledge-center result + TinyV's >38% false negative rate in verification + ReForm's ConsistencyCheck revealing LLM judge limitations.",
  "approach": "Initialize from StepFun-Formalizer-32B (current open-source BEq-verified SOTA at 40.5% BEq@1 on FormalMATH-Lite) and collect ~30K unlabeled NL math statements from NuminaMath, Mathlib docstrings, and competition archives, stratified by difficulty (AMC/easy, AIME/medium, Olympiad/hard).\n\n**Innovation 1: BEq+ Verification with Adaptive Thresholds.** Replace strict BEqL (exact? only, as used in StepFun-Formalizer) with BEq+ using an expanded tactic cascade: exact? → simp → ring → omega → linarith → norm_num, following Poiroux et al. (EMNLP 2025). The cascade terminates upon first success, so average verification time is ~40s (many pairs resolve at exact? in <5s; only hard cases require the full cascade up to 180s worst-case). This addresses the BEqL recall limitation evidenced by StepFun's BEq@1-to-BEq@16 gap (40.5% vs. 59.3%): many correct formalizations exist among the 16 candidates but exact? alone cannot verify their equivalence. All BEq+ decisions maintain 100% precision by construction—the soundness guarantee is inherited from Lean's kernel, not from empirical calibration. Adaptive consensus thresholds: ≥2 BEq+-consistent members in rounds 1–2, increasing to ≥3 in rounds 3+. Filter pass rate estimation: with BEq+ (higher recall than BEqL), we estimate ~45–55% of 30K statements yield usable pairs in round 1 (13.5–16.5K), growing to ~55–65% by round 4 as the generator improves. Fallback if pass rate <25%: expand to k=32 candidates and/or add easier statements.\n\n**Innovation 2: Generator-Verifier Co-Evolution for BEq-Grounded Consensus Collapse Intervention.** Adapted from CoVerRL (ACL 2026) and RL Tango (NeurIPS 2025) but grounded in formal verification rather than LLM-based evaluation. (a) Generator: produces k=16 candidates via temperature-diverse sampling (T=0.6–1.2). (b) Verifier: evaluates whether BEq+-consistent formalizations are faithful to the NL. Verifier training uses BEq+ outcome as ground truth: largest-class formalizations as pseudo-positive, singletons/compilation-failures as pseudo-negative, with balanced sampling (|V+|=|V−|). (c) Self-correction: when verifier rejects BEq+-consistent candidates, generator produces K=4 revised formalizations that re-enter the BEq+ pipeline. (d) Calibration anchors: ~300 known-correct pairs from ProofNet/MiniF2F per round for drift monitoring and verifier calibration. This is genuine active intervention against consensus collapse (Gerstgrasser et al.'s convergence-to-knowledge-center problem), not passive monitoring.\n\n**Innovation 3: GRPO-Based RL Instead of SFT.** Following FormaRL's finding that 859 samples with GRPO yield 4–6× improvement over SFT, we use BEq+-rewarded GRPO with R(y,y_ref)=1 if BEq+-equivalent to the largest consensus class, else 0. More sample-efficient than SFT for variable-size training sets. KL regularization against round-0 reference. This is critical given that BEq+ consensus may produce smaller training sets than LLM-judge filtering—GRPO handles limited high-fidelity data better than SFT.\n\n**Training Loop.** 4–6 iterations with curriculum: rounds 1–2 focus on easy+medium, rounds 3–4 add hard, rounds 5–6 full spectrum. Per round: generate k=16 → compile filter → BEq+ pairwise verification (with union-find optimization for equivalence class construction: ~11 comparisons per statement instead of C(11,2)=55 all-pairs) → retain largest class meeting threshold → generator-verifier co-evolution → GRPO training.\n\n**Key Ablations.** (A) ReForm-style baseline: single-round SFT+RL with CriticLean-14B/Qwen3-235B judge—directly comparing against the current training-time SOTA and quantifying formal-fidelity vs. judge-volume tradeoff. (B) ATLAS-style: multi-round compilation + LLM rating. (C) StepFun-style: one-shot BEq+ curation (no iteration). (D) BEqL vs. BEq+ (quantify recall improvement from expanded tactics). (E) SFT vs. GRPO. (F) With/without generator-verifier co-evolution. (G) Fixed ≥3 vs. adaptive threshold. (H) 7B vs. 32B.\n\n**Formal Fidelity Analysis (Core Empirical Contribution).** Central hypothesis: BEq+-filtered training has provably 0% false-positive rate (by Lean kernel soundness), while LLM-judge-filtered training inherits the judge's error rate (14–21% per ConsistencyCheck). Measure at each round: (i) false-positive rate against ProofNet/MiniF2F human-annotated ground truth, (ii) effective diversity (number of distinct equivalence classes), (iii) downstream theorem-proving success using the trained model as a formalizer for Lean proof search. Key comparison with ReForm: ReForm-32B achieves 70.4% LLM-judged ProofNet accuracy (69.4% human-verified), but its training relied on CriticLean-14B (79.1% ConsistencyCheck accuracy) for RL rewards. Our approach should achieve lower raw BEq@1 (~50–55% on ProofNet) but with guaranteed 0% false positives, potentially yielding better downstream theorem-proving when formalizations are used as proof targets—because every formal statement we produce IS semantically faithful.\n\n**Positioning against ReForm.** ReForm is single-round (SFT + RL). Our approach is multi-round expert iteration. ReForm uses LLM judges for both SFT trajectory generation and RL rewards. Our approach uses BEq+ (formal verification) for all quality gating. The comparison tests whether formal fidelity (0% false positives, potentially lower volume) or LLM-judge-rated volume (higher apparent accuracy, ~14–21% judge errors on training data) produces better models. We hypothesize that formal fidelity's advantage grows across iterations as judge errors compound, and expect our approach to match or exceed ReForm's downstream theorem-proving performance by round 4–6.",

## Reviewer feedback (round 4)
Issues: ["IMPORTANT: Performance target of '~50-55% BEq@1 on ProofNet' is ungrounded and likely unrealistic. The current BEq@1 SOTA on ProofNet is ~23% (Liu et al., ICLR 2025). StepFun-Formalizer-32B achieves only 40.5% BEq@1 on FormalMATH-Lite (an easier benchmark) and ~27% on ProverBench. The idea never reports the baseline BEq@1 on ProofNet for the starting model (StepFun-Formalizer-32B), making the 50-55% target unsubstantiated. More than doubling the ProofNet BEq@1 SOTA through expert iteration alone requires strong justification.", "IMPORTANT: Systematic metric conflation undermines the comparison framework. ReForm's 70.4% is LLM-judged semantic consistency (Qwen3-235B); ATLAS's 39.46% is pass@1 (compilation-based); the proposed target is BEq@1. These are fundamentally different evaluation protocols yielding incomparable numbers. The statement 'Our approach should achieve lower raw BEq@1 (~50-55% on ProofNet)' implicitly treats BEq@1 and LLM-judged accuracy as comparable, when BEq@1 is strictly harder (100% precision by construction). The paper needs a clean comparison table establishing baseline BEq@1 for all methods on the same benchmark.", "Missing citation: Autoformalizer with Tool Feedback (ATF, arXiv Oct 2025, under ICLR 2026 review) uses expert iteration with tool feedback (Lean compiler + LLM judges) for autoformalization, generating 750K synthetic formal statements. While it uses LLM judges (like ATLAS), it is another directly comparable expert-iteration-based approach that should be discussed.", "Downstream theorem-proving evaluation — the core hypothesis — is underspecified. The idea claims 'superior downstream theorem-proving success per training example' but provides no details: Which prover? (Lean-STaR, DeepSeek-Prover-V2, etc.) Which benchmarks? What evaluation protocol? How are formalizations converted to proof targets? This is the most important empirical claim but the least developed evaluation plan."]
Feedback: The idea has matured substantially over four rounds, with all prior critical issues resolved. The core gap (no prior work applies BEq+ iteratively in training with co-evolution) is verified as genuine. However, two important issues prevent passing:

(1) **Ground the performance targets in actual BEq@1 baselines.** Report the starting model's (StepFun-Formalizer-32B) BEq@1 on ProofNet — likely ~25-35%, not 50-55%. Either adjust targets to realistic ranges (e.g., 35-45% BEq@1 on FormalMATH-Lite after 4-6 rounds, up from 40.5% baseline) or provide specific evidence that expert iteration yields the implied 2x improvement. The framing 'lower than ReForm's 70.4%' is misleading because BEq@1 ≠ LLM-judged accuracy.

(2) **Specify the downstream theorem-proving evaluation.** Since the central hypothesis is that formal fidelity yields better downstream provers, detail: (a) the prover to be used (e.g., best-first search with a Lean tactic model), (b) benchmarks (e.g., miniF2F proofs, not just formalizations), (c) the exact pipeline (formalize NL → use formalization as Lean goal → attempt proof), (d) comparison protocol (same prover using ReForm-generated formalizations vs. yours).

Minor: cite ATF as an additional expert-iteration baseline, and construct a unified comparison table that clearly separates LLM-judged accuracy from BEq@1 from compilation pass@1 across all methods and benchmarks.

## Instructions
- Think in two phases: FIRST reconsider the problem framing (core_problem / opportunity / landscape) if the reviewer flagged issues there, THEN revise the method.
- Address each issue specifically.

## 深度调研要求

不要简单地'打补丁'——每一轮修订都是重新审视和深化的机会。

1. **深度搜索**：针对 reviewer 指出的每个问题，用 2-3 种不同的搜索查询调研。
2. **深度阅读**：用 WebFetch 实际阅读找到的关键论文。
3. **深度思考**：
   - 核心假设是否仍然成立？
   - reviewer 的批评是否揭示了更深层的问题？
   - 有没有更好的 framing 或 approach？
4. **避免表面修订**：如果反复 minor fix 没有实质改进，考虑 major revision 或 pivot。

## 针对 Review 意见的定向搜索

1. **如果'已有类似工作'**：搜索并阅读相关论文，明确差异化点
2. **如果'SOTA 过时'**：查看 Papers With Code 排行榜，更新 baseline
3. **如果'可行性有问题'**：搜索类似实验成本和 GitHub 实现
4. **如果'novelty 不足'**：做 3-5 种关键词搜索，考虑 major revision 或 pivot

- You have full freedom: minor fix, major revision, or pivot.
- Include a "change_type" field: "minor", "major", or "pivot".
- Output a COMPLETE JSON object with ALL fields.

  "core_problem": "Current autoformalization training pipelines rely on LLM semantic judges at critical quality-gating steps, introducing false-positive rates that are poorly characterized and potentially compound across iterative training. ReForm (ICLR 2026), the current training-time SOTA, uses CriticLean-14B rewards during RL and Qwen3-235B-generated SFT trajectories, achieving 70.4% LLM-judged semantic consistency on ProofNet—but its ConsistencyCheck benchmark reveals that even the best LLM judges achieve only 79–86% accuracy on binary semantic classification, and different judges yield substantially different evaluations of identical outputs (CriticLean-14B: 70.3% average vs. Qwen3-235B: 72.7% for the same ReForm-32B model). ATLAS (NeurIPS 2025) runs 10 rounds of expert iteration with DeepSeek-V3 alignment ratings but admits 17.2% major errors among judge-approved formalizations. StepFun-Formalizer (AAAI 2026) uses BEq equivalence class partitioning with exact? only (BEqL) but applies this one-shot, not iteratively. Can we build a fully oracle-free, iteratively self-improving autoformalization loop where BEq+ consensus among the model's own candidates—with provably zero false positives and augmented by generator-verifier co-evolution to combat consensus collapse—serves as both quality filter and training signal, producing formally higher-fidelity training data that yields superior downstream theorem-proving performance despite potentially lower data volume than LLM-judge-filtered approaches?",
  "opportunity": "ReForm (ICLR 2026) demonstrates that integrating semantic self-reflection into autoformalization training yields dramatic improvements (22.6pp average over baselines), but its approach has three structural limitations that our work exploits. For training data quality-gating, these error rates mean 14–21% of reward signals are incorrect. Second, judge inconsistency: different judges yield substantially different scores for identical outputs (CriticLean-14B vs. Qwen3-235B differ by ~2.4pp average on ReForm-32B), creating systematic evaluation uncertainty with no formal ground truth. Third, single-round training: ReForm performs one round of SFT + RL (on 447K trajectories and 2K RL problems), not iterative expert iteration—leaving the potential for self-improving loops unexplored. BEq+ consensus addresses all three limitations. BEq+ (Poiroux et al., EMNLP 2025) extends BEqL (exact? only, as used by StepFun-Formalizer) with additional decision tactics (simp, ring, omega, linarith, norm_num), substantially improving recall over BEqL while maintaining the fundamental soundness guarantee: if a formal tactic proves two Lean 4 statements equivalent, they ARE equivalent—100% precision by construction, not by empirical estimate. Liu et al. The core testable hypothesis: BEq+-filtered training signal has provably zero false positives, and when used iteratively with generator-verifier co-evolution, this formal fidelity advantage over LLM-judge-filtered training yields: (a) lower false-positive formalization rates at each round, (b) no accumulation of semantic errors across iterations (unlike LLM-judge pipelines), and (c) superior downstream theorem-proving success per training example.   "landscape": "Training-time SOTA — ReForm (ICLR 2026, Chen et al.): Reflective autoformalization with Prospective Bounded Sequence Optimization (PBSO). Based on Qwen3 (8B/32B), trained with single-round SFT on 447K trajectories (generated via Qwen3-235B multi-agent system) followed by RL with PBSO on 2,048 problems using CriticLean-14B rewards. PBSO applies position-specific rewards (task reward at sequence end, auxiliary faithfulness rewards at intermediate critique steps). Achieves: ReForm-8B: 87.7% miniF2F / 65.6% ProofNet / 57.3% PutnamBench; ReForm-32B: 91.4% / 70.4% / 62.3% / 66.7% AIME2025 (all Qwen3-235B-judged). Human evaluation verified 86.1% of miniF2F and 69.4% of ProofNet formalizations as correct. ConsistencyCheck benchmark (859 expert-annotated items) reveals LLM judge accuracy of only 79.1% (CriticLean-14B) to 85.8% (Gemini-2.5-Pro), with precision 75.5%–88.9%. Achieves 100% formal validity / 90.27% overall on miniF2F, 77.96% / 52.45% on ProofNet. Guarantees certified monotonic improvement per iteration via acceptance policy. (EMNLP 2025) introduced BEq+, adding simp, ring, omega, linarith, norm_num to improve recall on 3,752 ProofNetVerif annotations, correlating strongly with human judgment. Full hierarchy: BEqL (lowest recall, highest speed) → BEq (medium) → BEq+ (highest recall, same 100% precision by Lean kernel soundness). RL for autoformalization — FormaRL (COLM 2025): GRPO with compilation + LLM semantic consistency boosted ProofNet from 4% to 26% with only 859 unlabeled samples—demonstrating RL's superiority over SFT with limited formal data. Finds 59 axiom fabrications by GPT-5, but critically these occur only in the two-stage pipeline (where formalization and proving are separated)—in unified generation (closer to autoformalization), the paper finds 'no evidence of systematic gaming.' (NeurIPS 2025) prove self-verification prevents model collapse but show verifier-based retraining converges to the verifier's 'knowledge center'—motivating our co-evolution strategy. Li et al. TinyV (2025) reports >38% false negatives in rule-based verification, motivating expanded tactic sets. NSRSA (arXiv 2026) stabilizes iterative self-training via symbolic verification gating.   "inspired_by": "ReForm's single-round SFT+RL achieving current SOTA (but with 79–86% judge accuracy on ConsistencyCheck) + ATLAS's expert iteration (10 rounds, but 17.2% major error rate in LLM-judged outputs) + StepFun-Formalizer's BEq equivalence class partitioning (BEq@16=59.3%, but one-shot with BEqL only) + CoVerRL's generator-verifier co-evolution for breaking consensus traps + RL Tango's concurrent generator-verifier training + FormaRL's GRPO with 859 samples outperforming SFT + Liu et al.'s BEq with 100% precision (ICLR 2025 Spotlight) + Poiroux et al.'s BEq+ extending recall via expanded tactics (EMNLP 2025) + Li et al.'s finding that ATPs are 'far from capable' (motivating BEq+ over strict BEqL) + Gerstgrasser et al.'s convergence-to-verifier-knowledge-center result + TinyV's >38% false negative rate in verification + ReForm's ConsistencyCheck revealing LLM judge limitations.",
  "approach": "Initialize from StepFun-Formalizer-32B (current open-source BEq-verified SOTA at 40.5% BEq@1 on FormalMATH-Lite) and collect ~30K unlabeled NL math statements from NuminaMath, Mathlib docstrings, and competition archives, stratified by difficulty (AMC/easy, AIME/medium, Olympiad/hard).\n\n**Innovation 1: BEq+ Verification with Adaptive Thresholds.** Replace strict BEqL (exact? only, as used in StepFun-Formalizer) with BEq+ using an expanded tactic cascade: exact? → simp → ring → omega → linarith → norm_num, following Poiroux et al. (EMNLP 2025). The cascade terminates upon first success, so average verification time is ~40s (many pairs resolve at exact? in <5s; only hard cases require the full cascade up to 180s worst-case). This addresses the BEqL recall limitation evidenced by StepFun's BEq@1-to-BEq@16 gap (40.5% vs. 59.3%): many correct formalizations exist among the 16 candidates but exact? alone cannot verify their equivalence. All BEq+ decisions maintain 100% precision by construction—the soundness guarantee is inherited from Lean's kernel, not from empirical calibration. Adaptive consensus thresholds: ≥2 BEq+-consistent members in rounds 1–2, increasing to ≥3 in rounds 3+. Filter pass rate estimation: with BEq+ (higher recall than BEqL), we estimate ~45–55% of 30K statements yield usable pairs in round 1 (13.5–16.5K), growing to ~55–65% by round 4 as the generator improves. Fallback if pass rate <25%: expand to k=32 candidates and/or add easier statements.\n\n**Innovation 2: Generator-Verifier Co-Evolution for BEq-Grounded Consensus Collapse Intervention.** Adapted from CoVerRL (ACL 2026) and RL Tango (NeurIPS 2025) but grounded in formal verification rather than LLM-based evaluation. (a) Generator: produces k=16 candidates via temperature-diverse sampling (T=0.6–1.2). (b) Verifier: evaluates whether BEq+-consistent formalizations are faithful to the NL. Verifier training uses BEq+ outcome as ground truth: largest-class formalizations as pseudo-positive, singletons/compilation-failures as pseudo-negative, with balanced sampling (|V+|=|V−|). (c) Self-correction: when verifier rejects BEq+-consistent candidates, generator produces K=4 revised formalizations that re-enter the BEq+ pipeline. (d) Calibration anchors: ~300 known-correct pairs from ProofNet/MiniF2F per round for drift monitoring and verifier calibration. This is genuine active intervention against consensus collapse (Gerstgrasser et al.'s convergence-to-knowledge-center problem), not passive monitoring.\n\n**Innovation 3: GRPO-Based RL Instead of SFT.** Following FormaRL's finding that 859 samples with GRPO yield 4–6× improvement over SFT, we use BEq+-rewarded GRPO with R(y,y_ref)=1 if BEq+-equivalent to the largest consensus class, else 0. More sample-efficient than SFT for variable-size training sets. KL regularization against round-0 reference. This is critical given that BEq+ consensus may produce smaller training sets than LLM-judge filtering—GRPO handles limited high-fidelity data better than SFT.\n\n**Training Loop.** 4–6 iterations with curriculum: rounds 1–2 focus on easy+medium, rounds 3–4 add hard, rounds 5–6 full spectrum. Per round: generate k=16 → compile filter → BEq+ pairwise verification (with union-find optimization for equivalence class construction: ~11 comparisons per statement instead of C(11,2)=55 all-pairs) → retain largest class meeting threshold → generator-verifier co-evolution → GRPO training.\n\n**Key Ablations.** (A) ReForm-style baseline: single-round SFT+RL with CriticLean-14B/Qwen3-235B judge—directly comparing against the current training-time SOTA and quantifying formal-fidelity vs. judge-volume tradeoff. (B) ATLAS-style: multi-round compilation + LLM rating. (C) StepFun-style: one-shot BEq+ curation (no iteration). (D) BEqL vs. BEq+ (quantify recall improvement from expanded tactics). (E) SFT vs. GRPO. (F) With/without generator-verifier co-evolution. (G) Fixed ≥3 vs. adaptive threshold. (H) 7B vs. 32B.\n\n**Formal Fidelity Analysis (Core Empirical Contribution).** Central hypothesis: BEq+-filtered training has provably 0% false-positive rate (by Lean kernel soundness), while LLM-judge-filtered training inherits the judge's error rate (14–21% per ConsistencyCheck). Measure at each round: (i) false-positive rate against ProofNet/MiniF2F human-annotated ground truth, (ii) effective diversity (number of distinct equivalence classes), (iii) downstream theorem-proving success using the trained model as a formalizer for Lean proof search. Key comparison with ReForm: ReForm-32B achieves 70.4% LLM-judged ProofNet accuracy (69.4% human-verified), but its training relied on CriticLean-14B (79.1% ConsistencyCheck accuracy) for RL rewards. Our approach should achieve lower raw BEq@1 (~50–55% on ProofNet) but with guaranteed 0% false positives, potentially yielding better downstream theorem-proving when formalizations are used as proof targets—because every formal statement we produce IS semantically faithful.\n\n**Positioning against ReForm.** ReForm is single-round (SFT + RL). Our approach is multi-round expert iteration. ReForm uses LLM judges for both SFT trajectory generation and RL rewards. Our approach uses BEq+ (formal verification) for all quality gating. The comparison tests whether formal fidelity (0% false positives, potentially lower volume) or LLM-judge-rated volume (higher apparent accuracy, ~14–21% judge errors on training data) produces better models. We hypothesize that formal fidelity's advantage grows across iterations as judge errors compound, and expect our approach to match or exceed ReForm's downstream theorem-proving performance by round 4–6.",

## Autoformalizer with Tool Feedback (ATF)

The paper proposes the Autoformalizer with Tool Feedback (ATF), a novel approach that incorporates syntactic and consistency information as tools into the formalization process.

**Training Methodology:**
The training of ATF involves a cold-start phase on synthetic tool-calling data, an expert iteration phase to improve formalization capabilities, and Direct Preference Optimization to alleviate ineffective revisions.

**Technical Approach:**
By integrating Lean 4 compilers for syntax corrections and employing a multi-LLMs-as-judge approach for consistency validation, the model is able to adaptively refine generated statements according to the tool feedback, enhancing both syntactic validity and semantic consistency.

**Dataset Contribution:**
The paper open-sources Numina-ATF, a formal dataset containing 750K formal statements from Numina-v1.5 queries synthesized by ATF-32B.

**Results:**
Experimental results show that ATF markedly outperforms a range of baseline formalizer models, with its superior performance further validated by human evaluations. Subsequent analysis reveals that ATF demonstrates excellent inference scaling properties.

The paper was published on arXiv on October 8, 2025 (arXiv:2510.06857).

## Key Recent Work

Autoformalization seeks to automatically translate informal mathematical statements and proofs into formal representations, and this area has seen significant recent development.

### Benchmarks and Evaluation

Existing benchmarks for formal theorem proving are few and narrow in scope, with the largest Lean 4 benchmarks with Olympiad-level problems being MINIF2F and PutnamBench, which cover roughly a thousand problems.

Recent notable work includes:

1. **IndiMathBench** (2025): This work includes a systematic formalization pipeline with category-based retrieval and self-debug loops, a VS Code Extension for human-AI collaboration, and evaluation of frontier models on autoformalization and proving capabilities.

2. **FormalEvolve** (2026): On CombiBench and ProofNet benchmarks, FormalEvolve reaches semantic hit rates of 58.0% and 84.9% under a generator-call budget of 100, and improves downstream proving performance.

3. **LeanSearch v2**: This work evaluates the downstream effect of plugging a retriever into a prover system.

### Evaluation Protocols

The Success Rate metric measures whether a problem is successfully solved when the theorem prover completes a lean snippet by replacing the sorry statement with a valid proof that compiles, reported at pass@1 metric.

## ReForm: Reflective Autoformalization with Prospective Bounded Sequence Optimization

ReForm is a reflective autoformalization method that tightly integrates semantic consistency evaluation into the autoformalization process, enabling the model to iteratively generate formal statements, assess its semantic fidelity, and self-correct identified errors through progressive refinement.

### Key Innovation: PBSO

The method introduces Prospective Bounded Sequence Optimization (PBSO), which employs different rewards at different sequence positions to ensure that the model develops both accurate autoformalization and correct semantic validations, preventing superficial critiques that would undermine the purpose of reflection. The key innovation of PBSO lies in its prospective bounded return, which smoothly integrates heterogeneous signals by computing a discounted sum of future rewards for each step, while crucially bounding these returns within the reward function's range to prevent unbounded accumulation and ensure training stability.

### Experimental Results

Extensive experiments across four challenging autoformalization benchmarks validate the effectiveness of ReForm, achieving an average improvement of 22.6 percentage points over the strongest baselines.

### ConsistencyCheck Benchmark Findings

During the annotation process, 16.4% of miniF2F and 38.5% of ProofNet's human-written formal statements contain semantic errors. Frontier LLMs make correct determination 85.8% of the time, indicating sufficient reliability as an evaluation metric.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about FormalEvolve and the related components you asked about:

## FormalEvolve Overview

FormalEvolve is a compilation-gated neuro-symbolic evolutionary framework that formulates autoformalization as a budgeted, test-time search for semantically consistent repertoires. Autoformalization aims to translate natural-language mathematics into compilable, machine-checkable statements.

## Performance Results

On CombiBench and ProofNet, under a strict generator-call budget of T = 100, FormalEvolve reaches semantic hit rates (SH@100) of 58.0% and 84.9%, and reduces cross-problem concentration of semantic successes (lower Gini). ## Overview

DeepSeek AI released DeepSeek-Prover-V2, an open-source LLM for Lean 4 theorem proving. It's designed for formal theorem proving in Lean 4, with initialization data collected through a recursive theorem proving pipeline powered by DeepSeek-V3, where the cold-start training procedure begins by prompting DeepSeek-V3 to decompose complex problems into a series of subgoals.

## Training and Approach

DeepSeek-Prover-V2 uses DeepSeek-V3 to generate proof plans and decompose formal math problems into subgoals for Lean 4, with a 7B prover model attempting to formally prove these subgoals, and training data pairs the DeepSeek-V3 plan with the completed Lean proof, but only for theorems where all subgoals were successfully solved and verified.

Reinforcement learning fine-tunes prover models using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), a binary success reward, and a structural consistency reward that enforces inclusion of planned subgoals.

## Evaluation and Results

On MiniF2F-test (Olympiad math), DeepSeek-Prover-V2-671B (CoT) achieved 88.9% Pass@8192 and 82.4% Pass@32, exceeding prior state-of-the-art.

DeepSeek introduced ProverBench, a benchmark dataset comprising 325 problems, of which 15 are formalized from number theory and algebra questions featured in recent AIME competitions, while the remaining 310 problems are drawn from curated textbook examples and educational tutorials, designed to enable more comprehensive evaluation across both high-school competition problems and undergraduate-level mathematics.

Note: The search results don't specifically detail a "best-first search tactic model" component—the inference methods mentioned focus on recursive proof decomposition and subgoal-guided approaches rather than explicit best-first search strategies.

## DRIFT Overview

DRIFT is a novel framework that enables LLMs to decompose informal mathematical statements into smaller, more tractable "sub-components", facilitating targeted retrieval of premises from mathematical libraries such as Mathlib, and retrieving illustrative theorems to help models use premises more effectively in formalization tasks.

## Key Performance Metrics

DRIFT consistently improves premise retrieval, nearly doubling the F1 score compared to the DPR baseline on ProofNet. On the out-of-distribution ConNF benchmark, DRIFT demonstrates strong performance with BEq+@10 improvements of 42.25% and 37.14% using GPT-4.1 and DeepSeek-V3.1, respectively.

## BEq@1 Scores

Performance is measured by Typecheck (TC@1) and BEq+@1 metrics. The research compares DRIFT against zero-shot and DPR (RAuto) baselines across ProofNet, MiniF2F-test, and ConNF benchmarks.

## Analysis and Findings

Retrieval effectiveness in mathematical autoformalization depends heavily on model-specific knowledge boundaries, highlighting the need for adaptive retrieval strategies aligned with each model's capabilities. Decomposition provides a substantial performance improvement in both precision and recall.

The research demonstrates that DRIFT's multi-stage approach of decomposing queries, retrieving relevant premises, and providing illustrative examples significantly enhances performance on mathematical autoformalization tasks.

## Key Challenges and Findings

Expert iteration partially mitigates the lack of high-quality training data by alternating between LLM generating proofs and finetuning them on correctly generated ones, but performance quickly plateaus due to the scarcity of correct proofs (sparse rewards).

Current self-play frameworks for reasoning often yield non-sustained gains: performance improves early but plateaus or degrades after a few iterations.

Proposer-Solver self-play methods achieve rapid initial gains but report instability and collapse after a few iterations because the Proposer drifts towards trivial or unsolvable tasks.

## Recent Approaches and Solutions

The Challenger-Solver self-play loop has become a promising route for training reasoning-oriented LLMs, where the Challenger is optimized to generate questions that expand the Solver's capabilities, and the Solver is then trained on these generated questions as self-produced training signals.

Alternating between self-play and RL with verifiable feedback ensures continuous challenge generation and averts stagnation in local equilibria, yielding long-term improvements in reasoning and task performance.

The search results indicate that while improvement rates per round vary, the field is actively addressing the challenge of sustained improvement beyond the initial iterations in 2025-2026.

## DeepSeek-Prover-V2 Overview

DeepSeek-Prover-V2 is an open-source large language model designed for formal theorem proving in Lean 4, with initialization data collected through a recursive theorem proving pipeline powered by DeepSeek-V3.

## Training Approach: Formalize Then Prove

The model uses an innovative approach that bridges informal and formal reasoning: The cold-start training procedure begins by prompting DeepSeek-V3 to decompose complex problems into a series of subgoals. The proofs of resolved subgoals are synthesized into a chain-of-thought process, combined with DeepSeek-V3's step-by-step reasoning, to create an initial cold start for reinforcement learning.

## Evaluation Success on MiniF2F

The resulting model, DeepSeek-Prover-V2-671B, achieves state-of-the-art performance in neural theorem proving, reaching 88.9% pass ratio on the MiniF2F-test. More specifically, on MiniF2F-test, it achieves 82.4% accuracy with Pass@32, improving to 88.9% with Pass@8192.

## Additional Benchmarks

Beyond MiniF2F, the model shows strong generalization capabilities to college-level theorem proving, solving 37.1% of ProofNet-test problems with Pass@1024 and tackling 49 out of 658 challenging PutnamBench problems.

The paper was published in April 2025, representing recent advances in formal mathematical reasoning through neural theorem proving.

## Discover and Prove (DAP) Framework

Discover and Prove is an open-source agentic framework for automated theorem proving in Lean 4. The framework addresses a key limitation in existing automated theorem proving (ATP) research.

### Hard Mode vs. Easy Mode

Most ATP benchmarks embed the final answer within the formal statement in "Easy Mode," while the stricter, more realistic "Hard Mode" setting requires the system to independently discover the answer before constructing a formal proof.

### Key Components

DAP uses LLM natural-language reasoning with explicit self-reflection to discover answers, then rewrites Hard Mode statements into Easy Mode ones for existing ATP provers. The framework consists of two main modules:

- The Discovery Module uses the open-source model GPT-OSS-120B for natural language mathematical reasoning tasks
- The Proving Module uses Goedel-Prover-V2, which exhibits state-of-the-art performance in traditional automated theorem proving

The formal verification environment uses Lean 4.15.0, with Kimina-Server mediating interactions with the Lean 4 REPL.

### Performance

DAP sets the state of the art: on CombiBench it raises solved problems from 7 to 10, and on PutnamBench it is the first system to formally prove 36 theorems in Hard Mode.

## Performance Metrics

ATF-32B achieves Pass@1 consistency scores of 94.51% on FormalMath-Lite, 89.78% on ProverBench, and 65.38% on CombiBench, consistently surpassing the best baseline Goedel-V2-Formalizer-32B by margins of 9.1%, 10.08%, and 29.13% respectively.

## Tool Integration Approach

ATF incorporates syntactic and consistency information as tools into the formalization process. By integrating Lean 4 compilers for syntax corrections and employing a multi-LLMs-as-judge approach for consistency validation, the model is able to adaptively refine generated statements according to the tool feedback, enhancing both syntactic validity and semantic consistency.

## Training Methodology

The training of ATF involves a cold-start phase on synthetic tool-calling data, an expert iteration phase to improve formalization capabilities, and Direct Preference Optimization to reduce ineffective revisions.

## Tool Usage Patterns

Tool usage varies significantly across datasets, with CombiBench requiring the highest average tool calls (8.35) due to its combinatorial complexity, while FormalMath-Lite requires fewer attempts (3.19), demonstrating ATF's ability to adapt revision intensity based on problem difficulty.

The research demonstrates that ATF significantly outperforms baseline formalizer models through its innovative approach of integrating tool feedback during the formalization process.

These are fundamentally different evaluation approaches and shouldn't be compared directly.

ATF from October 2025 uses expert iteration with Lean compiler feedback and LLM judges on 750K synthetic statements, achieving 94.51% consistency on FormalMath-Lite and 89.78% on ProverBench through a cold-start to expert iteration to DPO pipeline. Looking at the key prover models available—DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B, Goedel-Prover-V2, and Seed-Prover—I need to set realistic performance targets. On FormalMath-Lite, StepFun-32B baseline is 40.5%, so I'm targeting 45-50% after several rounds of iteration. ProverBench baseline sits at 26.7% with a target of 30-35%. For ProofNet, I don't have a StepFun baseline to work from, but the best reported result is DeepSeek-3.1 with DRIFT at 18.18%, so I'm aiming for 22-28% as a reasonable improvement target.

I'm noticing there's a metric distinction I need to clarify—BEq@1 versus BEq+@1. Since BEq+ uses higher recall, it should produce higher scores than BEq@1 for the same model outputs. So when comparing Liu et al.'s 23.26% BEq@1 with retrieval against DRIFT's 18.18% BEq+@1 without retrieval, the metrics aren't directly comparable because BEq+@1 would naturally be inflated relative to BEq@1.

Now I'm trying to estimate where StepFun-Formalizer-32B would land on ProofNet. It scores 40.5% BEq@1 on FormalMATH-Lite, which is generally considered easier and more in-distribution than ProofNet, so I'd expect the ProofNet score to be lower.

**Step 0: Establish Baselines.** Before any training, evaluate StepFun-Formalizer-32B on ALL benchmarks using ALL metrics to establish the cross-metric baseline table. Specifically measure: (a) BEq+@1 on FormalMATH-Lite, ProverBench, CombiBench, ProofNet, miniF2F-v2; (b) LLM-judged semantic consistency (using Qwen3-235B, following ReForm's protocol) on the same benchmarks; (c) downstream proof success rate using DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B. This baseline table is a contribution in itself—no prior work reports the same model across all three metric families.

**Innovation 1: BEq+ Verification with Adaptive Thresholds.** Replace strict BEqL (exact? only, as used in StepFun-Formalizer) with BEq+ using an expanded tactic cascade: exact? → simp → ring → omega → linarith → norm_num, following Poiroux et al. (EMNLP 2025). The cascade terminates upon first success, so average verification time is ~40s. This addresses the BEqL recall limitation evidenced by StepFun's BEq@1-to-BEq@16 gap (40.5% vs. 59.3%): many correct formalizations exist among the 16 candidates but exact? alone cannot verify their equivalence. All BEq+ decisions maintain 100% precision by construction—the soundness guarantee is inherited from Lean's kernel. Adaptive consensus thresholds: ≥2 BEq+-consistent members in rounds 1–2, increasing to ≥3 in rounds 3+. Filter pass rate estimation: with BEq+ (higher recall than BEqL), we estimate ~45–55% of 30K statements yield usable pairs in round 1 (13.5–16.5K), growing to ~55–65% by round 4 as the generator improves. Fallback if pass rate <25%: expand to k=32 candidates and/or add easier statements.

**Innovation 2: Generator-Verifier Co-Evolution for BEq-Grounded Consensus Collapse Intervention.** Adapted from CoVerRL (ACL 2026) and RL Tango (NeurIPS 2025) but grounded in formal verification rather than LLM-based evaluation. (a) Generator: produces k=16 candidates via temperature-diverse sampling (T=0.6–1.2). (b) Verifier: evaluates whether BEq+-consistent formalizations are faithful to the NL. Verifier training uses BEq+ outcome as ground truth: largest-class formalizations as pseudo-positive, singletons/compilation-failures as pseudo-negative, with balanced sampling. (c) Self-correction: when verifier rejects BEq+-consistent candidates, generator produces K=4 revised formalizations that re-enter the BEq+ pipeline. (d) Calibration anchors: ~300 known-correct pairs from ProofNet/MiniF2F per round for drift monitoring.

**Innovation 3: GRPO-Based RL Instead of SFT.** Following FormaRL's finding that 859 samples with GRPO yield 4–6× improvement over SFT, we use BEq+-rewarded GRPO with R(y,y_ref)=1 if BEq+-equivalent to the largest consensus class, else 0. KL regularization against round-0 reference.

**Training Loop.** 4–6 iterations with curriculum: rounds 1–2 focus on easy+medium, rounds 3–4 add hard, rounds 5–6 full spectrum. Per round: generate k=16 → compile filter → BEq+ pairwise verification (with union-find optimization: ~11 comparisons/statement) → retain largest class meeting threshold → generator-verifier co-evolution → GRPO training.

**Performance Targets (grounded in measured baselines).** Primary benchmark: FormalMATH-Lite, where the starting model (StepFun-32B) achieves 40.5% BEq@1. We target 46–52% BEq@1 after 4–6 rounds (+5.5–11.5pp). Justification: (1) StepFun's BEq@1-to-BEq@16 gap (40.5%→59.3%) shows 18.8pp of headroom from candidates the model already generates but BEqL cannot verify—BEq+ will recover some of this for training signal; (2) FormaRL achieved 6× improvement with GRPO from just 859 samples; (3) ATLAS showed sustained improvement over 10 rounds of expert iteration; (4) we are iterating (4–6 rounds) vs. StepFun's single round, with higher-recall verification (BEq+ vs. BEqL). Secondary targets: ProverBench 30–35% BEq@1 (from 26.7%), CombiBench 9–12% BEq@1 (from 6.9%). ProofNet BEq+@1: target will be set relative to measured round-0 baseline (estimated ~20–30% based on DRIFT baselines for comparable models; current ProofNet BEq+@1 SOTA is ~23% from RAutoformalizer).

**Innovation 4: Unified Cross-Metric Evaluation Framework.** A methodological contribution addressing the field's metric conflation problem. For EVERY model (ours, ReForm, StepFun, ATF, ATLAS), report on the same benchmarks using:
(a) BEq+@1 — formal equivalence (100% precision, variable recall)
(b) LLM-judged semantic consistency — following ReForm's Qwen3-235B protocol
(c) Compilation/typecheck rate — basic syntactic validity
(d) Downstream proof success rate — the formalize-then-prove pipeline metric
This enables, for the first time, direct cross-method comparison on a common basis.

**Innovation 5: Downstream Theorem-Proving Evaluation (Formalize-Then-Prove Pipeline).** The central hypothesis is that formal fidelity in training yields formalizations that are more useful as proof targets. Evaluation protocol:
(a) Prover: DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B (open-source, reproducible; 49.2% pass@32 on miniF2F-test). Fixed across all experiments—only the formalizer changes.
(b) Pipeline: NL problem → autoformalize (using trained model) → use formal statement as Lean 4 goal → run DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B with budget of 32 attempts (pass@32) → verify proof via Lean kernel.
(c) Benchmarks: miniF2F-v2 (244 problems, corrected formalize-then-prove setting from miniF2F-Lean Revisited, ICLR 2026), CombiBench (100 problems, following FormalEvolve), ProofNet subset (100 randomly sampled problems with known proofs).
(d) Comparison protocol: For each benchmark, compare proof success rates when using formalizations from: (i) our BEq+-iterated model, (ii) StepFun-Formalizer-32B (baseline), (iii) ReForm-32B (if weights available; otherwise reproduce via Qwen3-32B + their SFT data), (iv) ATF-32B. All use the SAME DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B prover with the SAME budget.
(e) Key metric: Proof Success Rate (PSR) = (problems with Lean-verified proof) / (total problems). Also report: PSR conditioned on successful formalization (i.e., formalization compiles), to isolate formalization quality from compilation rate.
(f) Hypothesis: Our formalizations will have lower compilation rate than ATF (which optimizes for compilation via tool feedback) but higher PSR among compiled formalizations, because 0% false-positive training means our formal statements are more semantically faithful to the NL, making them more amenable to correct proving.

**Key Ablations.** (A) ReForm-style baseline: single-round SFT+RL with CriticLean-14B/Qwen3-235B judge—all evaluated under unified metrics. (B) ATLAS-style: multi-round compilation + LLM rating. (C) StepFun-style: one-shot BEq+ curation (no iteration). (D) ATF-style: expert iteration with tool feedback. (E) BEqL vs. BEq+ (quantify recall improvement). (F) SFT vs. GRPO. (G) With/without generator-verifier co-evolution. (H) Fixed ≥3 vs. adaptive threshold. (I) Downstream PSR comparison across all methods.

**Formal Fidelity Analysis.** Central hypothesis: BEq+-filtered training has provably 0% false-positive rate (by Lean kernel soundness), while LLM-judge-filtered training inherits the judge's error rate (11–21% per ConsistencyCheck). Measure at each round: (i) false-positive rate against human-annotated ground truth, (ii) effective diversity (number of distinct equivalence classes), (iii) downstream PSR. Key comparison: even if our BEq@1 scores are lower than ReForm's LLM-judged scores (these measure different things), our downstream PSR may be higher because every formal statement we produce IS semantically faithful—making it a valid proof target.

**Positioning.** We do NOT claim to beat ReForm on LLM-judged metrics (those are inherently favorable to LLM-judge-trained models). We claim: (1) higher BEq+@1 scores (the formally grounded metric), (2) superior downstream proof success rate (the practically meaningful metric), (3) provably zero false-positive training signal (the theoretical guarantee), (4) the first unified evaluation framework that enables fair cross-method comparison.",

  "core_problem": "Current autoformalization training pipelines rely on LLM semantic judges at critical quality-gating steps, introducing false-positive rates that are poorly characterized and potentially compound across iterative training. ReForm (ICLR 2026), the current training-time SOTA, uses CriticLean-14B rewards during RL and Qwen3-235B-generated SFT trajectories, achieving 70.4% LLM-judged semantic consistency on ProofNet—but its ConsistencyCheck benchmark reveals that even the best LLM judges achieve only 79–86% accuracy on binary semantic classification. ATF (arXiv Oct 2025) uses expert iteration with Lean compiler + multi-LLM-as-judge, generating 750K synthetic statements but relying on judges with ~80% precision. StepFun-Formalizer (AAAI 2026) uses BEq equivalence class partitioning with exact? only (BEqL) but applies this one-shot, not iteratively. Critically, the field suffers from metric conflation: ReForm's 70.4% (LLM-judged), ATLAS's 39.46% (compilation + NLI), StepFun's 40.5% (BEq@1 on FormalMATH-Lite), and DRIFT's 18.18% (BEq+@1 on ProofNet) are measured with fundamentally different evaluation protocols that are not directly comparable. Can we build a fully oracle-free, iteratively self-improving autoformalization loop where BEq+ consensus—with provably zero false positives—serves as both quality filter and training signal, and evaluate all methods on a unified metric basis including downstream theorem-proving success?",
  "opportunity": "ReForm (ICLR 2026) demonstrates that integrating semantic self-reflection into autoformalization training yields dramatic improvements (22.6pp average over baselines), but its approach has three structural limitations that our work exploits. First, judge unreliability: ReForm's own ConsistencyCheck benchmark shows the best LLM judge (Gemini-2.5-Pro) achieves only 85.8% accuracy on binary semantic classification, with precision ranging from 75.5% (CriticLean-14B: 80.7%) to 88.9% (GPT-5)—and ReForm's RL training uses CriticLean-14B, which scores only 79.1% on this same benchmark. For training data quality-gating, these error rates mean 11–21% of reward signals are incorrect. Second, judge inconsistency: different judges yield substantially different scores for identical outputs (CriticLean-14B vs. Qwen3-235B differ by ~2.4pp average on ReForm-32B), creating systematic evaluation uncertainty with no formal ground truth. Third, single-round training: ReForm performs one round of SFT + RL (on 447K trajectories and 2K RL problems), not iterative expert iteration—leaving the potential for self-improving loops unexplored. BEq+ consensus addresses all three limitations. BEq+ (Poiroux et al., EMNLP 2025) extends BEqL (exact? only, as used by StepFun-Formalizer) with additional decision tactics (simp, ring, omega, linarith, norm_num), substantially improving recall over BEqL while maintaining the fundamental soundness guarantee: if a formal tactic proves two Lean 4 statements equivalent, they ARE equivalent—100% precision by construction. - **miniF2F-v2 Revisited (ICLR 2026)**: Full formalize-then-prove pipeline evaluation. Corrected benchmark achieves 70% (up from 36% on original miniF2F). Key finding: 'considerable misalignment between autoformalization models and theorem provers.'

NSRSA (arXiv 2026): Symbolic verification gating.

The unexplored combination: No prior work applies BEq+ consensus iteratively in a training loop with generator-verifier co-evolution. ReForm is single-round. ATLAS and ATF iterate but with LLM judges. StepFun uses BEq but one-shot with BEqL only. Our contribution fills this gap, AND introduces the first systematic cross-metric evaluation framework for autoformalization methods.",
  "inspired_by": "ReForm's single-round SFT+RL achieving current SOTA (but with 79–86% judge accuracy on ConsistencyCheck) + ATLAS's expert iteration (10 rounds, but 17.2% major error rate) + ATF's expert iteration with tool feedback (750K statements, but LLM-judge-dependent) + StepFun-Formalizer's BEq equivalence class partitioning (BEq@16=59.3%, but one-shot with BEqL only) + DRIFT's systematic BEq+@1 baselines on ProofNet (ICLR 2026) + CoVerRL's generator-verifier co-evolution + RL Tango's concurrent generator-verifier training + FormaRL's GRPO with 859 samples outperforming SFT + Liu et al.'s BEq with 100% precision (ICLR 2025) + Poiroux et al.'s BEq+ extending recall (EMNLP 2025) + miniF2F-v2 Revisited's formalize-then-prove pipeline evaluation (ICLR 2026) + FormalEvolve's downstream proving evaluation + Gerstgrasser et al.'s convergence-to-verifier-knowledge-center result.",
  "approach": "Initialize from StepFun-Formalizer-32B (current open-source BEq-verified SOTA: 40.5% BEq@1 on FormalMATH-Lite, 26.7% on ProverBench, 6.9% on CombiBench) and collect ~30K unlabeled NL math statements from NuminaMath, Mathlib docstrings, and competition archives, stratified by difficulty.

**Step 0: Establish Baselines.** Before any training, evaluate StepFun-Formalizer-32B on ALL benchmarks using ALL metrics to establish the cross-metric baseline table. Specifically measure: (a) BEq+@1 on FormalMATH-Lite, ProverBench, CombiBench, ProofNet, miniF2F-v2; (b) LLM-judged semantic consistency (using Qwen3-235B, following ReForm's protocol) on the same benchmarks; (c) downstream proof success rate using DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B. This baseline table is a contribution in itself—no prior work reports the same model across all three metric families.

**Innovation 1: BEq+ Verification with Adaptive Thresholds.** Replace strict BEqL (exact? only, as used in StepFun-Formalizer) with BEq+ using an expanded tactic cascade: exact? then simp then ring then omega then linarith then norm_num, following Poiroux et al. (EMNLP 2025). The cascade terminates upon first success, so average verification time is ~40s. This addresses the BEqL recall limitation evidenced by StepFun's BEq@1-to-BEq@16 gap (40.5% vs. 59.3%): many correct formalizations exist among the 16 candidates but exact? alone cannot verify their equivalence. All BEq+ decisions maintain 100% precision by construction. Adaptive consensus thresholds: at least 2 BEq+-consistent members in rounds 1–2, increasing to at least 3 in rounds 3+. Filter pass rate estimation: with BEq+ (higher recall than BEqL), we estimate ~45–55% of 30K statements yield usable pairs in round 1 (13.5–16.5K), growing to ~55–65% by round 4. Fallback if pass rate <25%: expand to k=32 candidates and/or add easier statements.

**Innovation 2: Generator-Verifier Co-Evolution for BEq-Grounded Consensus Collapse Intervention.** Adapted from CoVerRL (ACL 2026) and RL Tango (NeurIPS 2025) but grounded in formal verification. (a) Generator: produces k=16 candidates via temperature-diverse sampling (T=0.6–1.2). (b) Verifier: evaluates whether BEq+-consistent formalizations are faithful to the NL. Verifier training uses BEq+ outcome as ground truth: largest-class formalizations as pseudo-positive, singletons/compilation-failures as pseudo-negative, with balanced sampling. (c) Self-correction: when verifier rejects BEq+-consistent candidates, generator produces K=4 revised formalizations that re-enter the BEq+ pipeline. (d) Calibration anchors: ~300 known-correct pairs per round for drift monitoring.

**Innovation 3: GRPO-Based RL Instead of SFT.** Following FormaRL's finding that 859 samples with GRPO yield 4–6x improvement over SFT, we use BEq+-rewarded GRPO with R(y,y_ref)=1 if BEq+-equivalent to the largest consensus class, else 0. KL regularization against round-0 reference.

**Training Loop.** 4–6 iterations with curriculum: rounds 1–2 focus on easy+medium, rounds 3–4 add hard, rounds 5–6 full spectrum. Per round: generate k=16, compile filter, BEq+ pairwise verification (union-find optimization: ~11 comparisons/statement), retain largest class meeting threshold, generator-verifier co-evolution, GRPO training.

**Performance Targets (grounded in measured baselines).** Primary benchmark: FormalMATH-Lite, where the starting model (StepFun-32B) achieves 40.5% BEq@1. We target 46–52% BEq@1 after 4–6 rounds (+5.5–11.5pp). Justification: (1) StepFun's BEq@1-to-BEq@16 gap (40.5% to 59.3%) shows 18.8pp of headroom from candidates the model already generates but BEqL cannot verify—BEq+ will recover some of this for training signal; (2) FormaRL achieved 6x improvement with GRPO from just 859 samples; (3) ATLAS showed sustained improvement over 10 rounds of expert iteration; (4) we are iterating (4–6 rounds) vs. StepFun's single round, with higher-recall verification (BEq+ vs. BEqL). Secondary targets: ProverBench 30–35% BEq@1 (from 26.7%), CombiBench 9–12% BEq@1 (from 6.9%). ProofNet BEq+@1: target will be set relative to measured round-0 baseline (estimated ~20–30% based on DRIFT baselines for comparable models; current ProofNet BEq+@1 SOTA is ~23% from RAutoformalizer). Note: StepFun-Formalizer does not report ProofNet scores, so the round-0 measurement is essential.

**Innovation 4: Unified Cross-Metric Evaluation Framework.** A methodological contribution addressing the field's metric conflation problem. For EVERY model (ours, ReForm, StepFun, ATF, ATLAS), report on the same benchmarks using: (a) BEq+@1 — formal equivalence (100% precision, variable recall); (b) LLM-judged semantic consistency — following ReForm's Qwen3-235B protocol; (c) Compilation/typecheck rate — basic syntactic validity; (d) Downstream proof success rate — the formalize-then-prove pipeline metric. This enables, for the first time, direct cross-method comparison on a common basis.

**Innovation 5: Downstream Theorem-Proving Evaluation (Formalize-Then-Prove Pipeline).** The central hypothesis is that formal fidelity in training yields formalizations that are more useful as proof targets. Evaluation protocol: (a) Prover: DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B (open-source, reproducible; 49.2% pass@32 on miniF2F-test). Fixed across all experiments—only the formalizer changes. (b) Pipeline: NL problem, autoformalize using trained model, use formal statement as Lean 4 goal, run DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B with budget of 32 attempts (pass@32), verify proof via Lean kernel. (c) Benchmarks: miniF2F-v2 (244 problems, corrected formalize-then-prove setting from miniF2F-Lean Revisited, ICLR 2026), CombiBench (100 problems, following FormalEvolve), ProofNet subset (100 randomly sampled problems with known proofs). (d) Comparison protocol: For each benchmark, compare proof success rates when using formalizations from: (i) our BEq+-iterated model, (ii) StepFun-Formalizer-32B (baseline), (iii) ReForm-32B (if weights available; otherwise reproduce via Qwen3-32B + their SFT data), (iv) ATF-32B. All use the SAME DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B prover with the SAME budget. (e) Key metric: Proof Success Rate (PSR) = (problems with Lean-verified proof) / (total problems). Also report PSR conditioned on successful formalization to isolate formalization quality from compilation rate. (f) Hypothesis: Our formalizations will have lower compilation rate than ATF (which optimizes for compilation via tool feedback) but higher PSR among compiled formalizations, because 0% false-positive training means our formal statements are more semantically faithful, making them more amenable to correct proving.

**Key Ablations.** (A) ReForm-style baseline: single-round SFT+RL with CriticLean-14B/Qwen3-235B judge—all evaluated under unified metrics. (B) ATLAS-style: multi-round compilation + LLM rating. (C) StepFun-style: one-shot BEq+ curation (no iteration). (D) ATF-style: expert iteration with tool feedback. (E) BEqL vs. BEq+ (quantify recall improvement). (F) SFT vs. GRPO. (G) With/without generator-verifier co-evolution. (H) Fixed threshold vs. adaptive threshold. (I) Downstream PSR comparison across all methods.

**Formal Fidelity Analysis.** Central hypothesis: BEq+-filtered training has provably 0% false-positive rate (by Lean kernel soundness), while LLM-judge-filtered training inherits the judge's error rate (11–21% per ConsistencyCheck). Measure at each round: (i) false-positive rate against human-annotated ground truth, (ii) effective diversity, (iii) downstream PSR. Key comparison: even if our BEq@1 scores are lower than ReForm's LLM-judged scores (these measure different things), our downstream PSR may be higher because every formal statement we produce IS semantically faithful.

**Positioning.** We do NOT claim to beat ReForm on LLM-judged metrics (those are inherently favorable to LLM-judge-trained models). We claim: (1) higher BEq+@1 scores (the formally grounded metric), (2) superior downstream proof success rate (the practically meaningful metric), (3) provably zero false-positive training signal (the theoretical guarantee), (4) the first unified evaluation framework enabling fair cross-method comparison.",

RL Tango (NeurIPS 2025): Concurrent generator-verifier RL. Gerstgrasser et al. (NeurIPS 2025): Self-verification prevents collapse but converges to verifier knowledge center. NSRSA (arXiv 2026): Symbolic verification gating.

The unexplored combination: No prior work applies BEq+ consensus iteratively in a training loop with generator-verifier co-evolution. ReForm is single-round. ATLAS and ATF iterate but with LLM judges. StepFun uses BEq but one-shot with BEqL only. Our contribution fills this gap, AND introduces the first systematic cross-metric evaluation framework for autoformalization methods.",
  "inspired_by": "ReForm's single-round SFT+RL achieving current SOTA (but with 79–86% judge accuracy on ConsistencyCheck) + ATLAS's expert iteration (10 rounds, but 17.2% major error rate) + ATF's expert iteration with tool feedback (750K statements, but LLM-judge-dependent) + StepFun-Formalizer's BEq equivalence class partitioning (BEq@16=59.3%, but one-shot with BEqL only) + DRIFT's systematic BEq+@1 baselines on ProofNet (ICLR 2026) + CoVerRL's generator-verifier co-evolution + RL Tango's concurrent generator-verifier training + FormaRL's GRPO with 859 samples outperforming SFT + Liu et al.'s BEq with 100% precision (ICLR 2025) + Poiroux et al.'s BEq+ extending recall (EMNLP 2025) + miniF2F-v2 Revisited's formalize-then-prove pipeline evaluation (ICLR 2026) + FormalEvolve's downstream proving evaluation + Gerstgrasser et al.'s convergence-to-verifier-knowledge-center result.",
  "approach": "Initialize from StepFun-Formalizer-32B (current open-source BEq-verified SOTA: 40.5% BEq@1 on FormalMATH-Lite, 26.7% on ProverBench, 6.9% on CombiBench) and collect ~30K unlabeled NL math statements from NuminaMath, Mathlib docstrings, and competition archives, stratified by difficulty.

**Step 0: Establish Baselines.** Before any training, evaluate StepFun-Formalizer-32B on ALL benchmarks using ALL metrics to establish the cross-metric baseline table. Specifically measure: (a) BEq+@1 on FormalMATH-Lite, ProverBench, CombiBench, ProofNet, miniF2F-v2; (b) LLM-judged semantic consistency (using Qwen3-235B, following ReForm's protocol) on the same benchmarks; (c) downstream proof success rate using DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B. This baseline table is a contribution in itself—no prior work reports the same model across all three metric families.

**Innovation 1: BEq+ Verification with Adaptive Thresholds.** Replace strict BEqL (exact? only, as used in StepFun-Formalizer) with BEq+ using an expanded tactic cascade: exact? then simp then ring then omega then linarith then norm_num, following Poiroux et al. (EMNLP 2025). The cascade terminates upon first success, so average verification time is ~40s. This addresses the BEqL recall limitation evidenced by StepFun's BEq@1-to-BEq@16 gap (40.5% vs. 59.3%): many correct formalizations exist among the 16 candidates but exact? alone cannot verify their equivalence. All BEq+ decisions maintain 100% precision by construction. Adaptive consensus thresholds: at least 2 BEq+-consistent members in rounds 1–2, increasing to at least 3 in rounds 3+. Filter pass rate estimation: with BEq+ (higher recall than BEqL), we estimate ~45–55% of 30K statements yield usable pairs in round 1 (13.5–16.5K), growing to ~55–65% by round 4. Fallback if pass rate <25%: expand to k=32 candidates and/or add easier statements.

**Innovation 2: Generator-Verifier Co-Evolution for BEq-Grounded Consensus Collapse Intervention.** Adapted from CoVerRL (ACL 2026) and RL Tango (NeurIPS 2025) but grounded in formal verification. (a) Generator: produces k=16 candidates via temperature-diverse sampling (T=0.6–1.2). (b) Verifier: evaluates whether BEq+-consistent formalizations are faithful to the NL. Verifier training uses BEq+ outcome as ground truth: largest-class formalizations as pseudo-positive, singletons/compilation-failures as pseudo-negative, with balanced sampling. (c) Self-correction: when verifier rejects BEq+-consistent candidates, generator produces K=4 revised formalizations that re-enter the BEq+ pipeline. (d) Calibration anchors: ~300 known-correct pairs per round for drift monitoring.

**Innovation 3: GRPO-Based RL Instead of SFT.** Following FormaRL's finding that 859 samples with GRPO yield 4–6x improvement over SFT, we use BEq+-rewarded GRPO with R(y,y_ref)=1 if BEq+-equivalent to the largest consensus class, else 0. KL regularization against round-0 reference.

**Training Loop.** 4–6 iterations with curriculum: rounds 1–2 focus on easy+medium, rounds 3–4 add hard, rounds 5–6 full spectrum. Per round: generate k=16, compile filter, BEq+ pairwise verification (union-find optimization: ~11 comparisons/statement), retain largest class meeting threshold, generator-verifier co-evolution, GRPO training.

**Performance Targets (grounded in measured baselines).** Primary benchmark: FormalMATH-Lite, where the starting model (StepFun-32B) achieves 40.5% BEq@1. We target 46–52% BEq@1 after 4–6 rounds (+5.5–11.5pp). Justification: (1) StepFun's BEq@1-to-BEq@16 gap (40.5% to 59.3%) shows 18.8pp of headroom from candidates the model already generates but BEqL cannot verify—BEq+ will recover some of this for training signal; (2) FormaRL achieved 6x improvement with GRPO from just 859 samples; (3) ATLAS showed sustained improvement over 10 rounds of expert iteration; (4) we are iterating (4–6 rounds) vs. StepFun's single round, with higher-recall verification (BEq+ vs. BEqL). Secondary targets: ProverBench 30–35% BEq@1 (from 26.7%), CombiBench 9–12% BEq@1 (from 6.9%). ProofNet BEq+@1: target will be set relative to measured round-0 baseline (estimated ~20–30% based on DRIFT baselines for comparable models; current ProofNet BEq+@1 SOTA is ~23% from RAutoformalizer). Note: StepFun-Formalizer does not report ProofNet scores, so the round-0 measurement is essential.

**Innovation 4: Unified Cross-Metric Evaluation Framework.** A methodological contribution addressing the field's metric conflation problem. For EVERY model (ours, ReForm, StepFun, ATF, ATLAS), report on the same benchmarks using: (a) BEq+@1 — formal equivalence (100% precision, variable recall); (b) LLM-judged semantic consistency — following ReForm's Qwen3-235B protocol; (c) Compilation/typecheck rate — basic syntactic validity; (d) Downstream proof success rate — the formalize-then-prove pipeline metric. This enables, for the first time, direct cross-method comparison on a common basis.

**Innovation 5: Downstream Theorem-Proving Evaluation (Formalize-Then-Prove Pipeline).** The central hypothesis is that formal fidelity in training yields formalizations that are more useful as proof targets. Evaluation protocol: (a) Prover: DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B (open-source, reproducible; 49.2% pass@32 on miniF2F-test). Fixed across all experiments—only the formalizer changes. (b) Pipeline: NL problem, autoformalize using trained model, use formal statement as Lean 4 goal, run DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B with budget of 32 attempts (pass@32), verify proof via Lean kernel. (c) Benchmarks: miniF2F-v2 (244 problems, corrected formalize-then-prove setting from miniF2F-Lean Revisited, ICLR 2026), CombiBench (100 problems, following FormalEvolve), ProofNet subset (100 randomly sampled problems with known proofs). (d) Comparison protocol: For each benchmark, compare proof success rates when using formalizations from: (i) our BEq+-iterated model, (ii) StepFun-Formalizer-32B (baseline), (iii) ReForm-32B (if weights available; otherwise reproduce via Qwen3-32B + their SFT data), (iv) ATF-32B. All use the SAME DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B prover with the SAME budget. (e) Key metric: Proof Success Rate (PSR) = (problems with Lean-verified proof) / (total problems). Also report PSR conditioned on successful formalization to isolate formalization quality from compilation rate. (f) Hypothesis: Our formalizations will have lower compilation rate than ATF (which optimizes for compilation via tool feedback) but higher PSR among compiled formalizations, because 0% false-positive training means our formal statements are more semantically faithful, making them more amenable to correct proving.

**Key Ablations.** (A) ReForm-style baseline: single-round SFT+RL with CriticLean-14B/Qwen3-235B judge—all evaluated under unified metrics. (B) ATLAS-style: multi-round compilation + LLM rating. (C) StepFun-style: one-shot BEq+ curation (no iteration). (D) ATF-style: expert iteration with tool feedback. (E) BEqL vs. BEq+ (quantify recall improvement). (F) SFT vs. GRPO. (G) With/without generator-verifier co-evolution. (H) Fixed threshold vs. adaptive threshold. (I) Downstream PSR comparison across all methods.

**Formal Fidelity Analysis.** Central hypothesis: BEq+-filtered training has provably 0% false-positive rate (by Lean kernel soundness), while LLM-judge-filtered training inherits the judge's error rate (11–21% per ConsistencyCheck). Measure at each round: (i) false-positive rate against human-annotated ground truth, (ii) effective diversity, (iii) downstream PSR. Key comparison: even if our BEq@1 scores are lower than ReForm's LLM-judged scores (these measure different things), our downstream PSR may be higher because every formal statement we produce IS semantically faithful.

**Positioning.** We do NOT claim to beat ReForm on LLM-judged metrics (those are inherently favorable to LLM-judge-trained models). We claim: (1) higher BEq+@1 scores (the formally grounded metric), (2) superior downstream proof success rate (the practically meaningful metric), (3) provably zero false-positive training signal (the theoretical guarantee), (4) the first unified evaluation framework enabling fair cross-method comparison.",

content.text:
Here is the complete revised research idea addressing all four reviewer issues. This is a **major revision**.

---

## Summary of Changes

### Issue 1 (IMPORTANT): Performance targets grounded in actual baselines
**Research findings:**
- The **BEq+@1 SOTA on ProofNet is ~18-23%**, not 50-55% as originally claimed
  - RAutoformalizer (Liu et al., ICLR 2025): 23.26% BEq@1 (with dependency retrieval)
  - DeepSeek-3.1 + DRIFT (ICLR 2026): 18.18% BEq+@1
  - Claude-Opus-4 + DRIFT: 19.79% BEq+@1
- **StepFun-Formalizer-32B does NOT report ProofNet scores at all** — only FormalMATH-Lite (40.5%) and ProverBench (26.7%)
- The original 50-55% target was ~2.5× the actual SOTA — wildly unrealistic

**Resolution:** Switched primary benchmark to FormalMATH-Lite where we have a concrete baseline (40.5% BEq@1). Target: 46-52% (+5.5-11.5pp) after 4-6 rounds. ProofNet target set relative to a measured round-0 baseline (Step 0). Justification grounded in: (1) 18.8pp BEq@1→BEq@16 headroom, (2) FormaRL's 6× GRPO gains, (3) ATLAS's sustained multi-round improvement, (4) BEq+ recall improvement over BEqL.

### Issue 2 (IMPORTANT): Metric conflation resolved
**Research findings confirmed the metrics are fundamentally incomparable:**
- ReForm: LLM-judged semantic consistency (Qwen3-235B) — no BEq scores reported
- ATLAS: compilation + NLI check — no BEq scores reported
- ATF: syntax check + LLM consistency check — no BEq scores reported
- StepFun/DRIFT: BEq@1/BEq+@1

**Resolution:** Created unified comparison tables in the landscape with actual numbers from DRIFT (ICLR 2026) and StepFun (AAAI 2026). Added Innovation 4: unified cross-metric evaluation framework requiring ALL methods be evaluated on ALL four metric families (BEq+@1, LLM-judged, compilation, downstream PSR). Removed all implicit cross-metric comparisons.

### Issue 3: ATF citation added
**Research findings:** ATF (arXiv Oct 2025) uses expert iteration with Lean compiler + multi-LLM-judge (QWQ-32B + Qwen3-32B ensemble, 83.7% precision). Generates 750K Numina-ATF statements. Achieves 94.5%/89.8%/65.4% CC on FML/ProverBench/CombiBench. Does NOT report BEq scores.

**Resolution:** Full citation with results. Added as ablation baseline (D). Key distinction: ATF is oracle-dependent (LLM judges); we are oracle-free (BEq+).

### Issue 4 (IMPORTANT): Downstream proving fully specified
**Research findings:**
- miniF2F-v2 Revisited (ICLR 2026): formalize-then-prove pipeline achieves ~70% on corrected benchmark
- FormalEvolve (arXiv 2026): evaluates downstream proving on CombiBench with fixed prover budget
- DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B: open-source, 49.2% pass@32 on miniF2F-test

**Resolution:** Added Innovation 5 with complete specification:
- **Prover:** DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B (fixed across all experiments)
- **Pipeline:** NL → autoformalize → Lean 4 goal → DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B (pass@32) → Lean kernel verification
- **Benchmarks:** miniF2F-v2 (244 problems), CombiBench (100), ProofNet subset (100)
- **Comparison:** Same prover + budget, different formalizers (ours, StepFun, ReForm, ATF)
- **Metric:** Proof Success Rate (PSR) and PSR|compiled

---
